sweep_summary: Single target item (Dąbkowski 2019, The morphophonology of A'ingae verbal stress; Glottolog 586673) located as an open PDF on LingBuzz (005879), downloaded (109 pp, text layer) and read. It is squarely about word stress in this language (verbs): default penultimate stress on lexically stressless verbs, a lexical class with word-initial stress, moraic weight with a glottal stop attracting stress to the syllable holding the second mora to its left, and four suffix cophonologies; it states that Borman 1962/1976 'find support in my data'. Also downloaded its peer-reviewed successor (Dąbkowski 2021, Phonology 38(4), lingbuzz/006445) and re-read the already-on-disk Dąbkowski 2024 Compass overview, 2025 dissertation and Repetti-Ludlow et al. 2019 JIPA sketch; all agree. classification on the catalog: the 'weight-hedged' coding from Borman 1962 ('usually penultimate or earlier') is refined, not contradicted — default penultimate, lexical initial exceptions, mora-sensitive glottal rule, morphological conditioning. Recommended new deciding source: Dąbkowski 2024 (Compass, CC-BY) §6.1-6.2 pp. 16-18, with the 2019 thesis / 2021 Phonology / 2025 dissertation as first-hand support. Three further LingBuzz manuscripts by the same author (005886, 005938, 005983) were seen as records only and not downloaded (low priority; content subsumed by the works held by the project).

new_statements.quote: Roots can be classified as plain (54i), stressed (54ii), or glottalised (54iii) … The first category consists of roots that do not have underlying stress. On the surface, underlyingly stressless forms receive default penultimate stress (54a.i). The second category contains roots that have underlying stress on the first syllable. … The third category includes roots with a glottal stop. The glottal stop surfaces in the coda of the penultimate syllable. On the surface, stress is regularly assigned to the syllable which contains the second mora to the left of the glottal stop.

new_statements.reading: Default word stress is penultimate (culminative, one peak per phonological word); a lexically listed class of roots carries fixed initial stress; roots with a glottal stop are stressed on the syllable containing the second mora to the left of the glottal stop (weight is moraic: diphthongs are bimoraic, so a heavy final root syllable can be stressed); in morphologically complex words stress is determined by suffix class (inner/outer × recessive/dominant/glottalised). Stress is essentially never word-final except in monosyllables. This is a first-hand, peer-reviewed, open-access overview by the fieldworker who wrote the 2019 thesis (the works with stress in the title), the 2021 Phonology paper and the 2025 dissertation; all four agree. The 2019 thesis states the same for verbs at pp. 40-42 ('Penultimate stress is the language's default assigned to verbs without lexical stress') and pp. 2/10 (glottal-stop mora rule), and the 2021 Phonology postprint at p. 5 ('By default, A'ingae primary stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable of the word'). Relative to the catalog's Borman 1962 'usually penultimate or earlier' this is a refinement, not a contradiction: it resolves the hedge into default penultimate + lexical initial exceptions + a mora-counting glottal rule + morphological conditioning.

sources.quote: Each phonological word has exactly one primary stress peak. The position of stress is contrastive in roots (52a–b) and in morphologically complex forms (52c–d) [p. 16] … Roots can be classified as plain (54i), stressed (54ii), or glottalised (54iii) … On the surface, underlyingly stressless forms receive default penultimate stress (54a.i). The second category contains roots that have underlying stress on the first syllable. … The third category includes roots with a glottal stop. The glottal stop surfaces in the coda of the penultimate syllable. On the surface, stress is regularly assigned to the syllable which contains the second mora to the left of the glottal stop. [p. 18]
sources.note: General (not verb-only) statement: one culminative primary stress per phonological word; default penultimate on stressless roots; a lexical class with initial stress; glottalised roots stressed on the syllable holding the second mora left of the glottal stop; suffix classes (inner/outer × recessive/dominant/glottalised) govern stress in complex words. Stress correlates with duration and often higher F0.

sources.quote: In bare disyllables, stress is uniformly penultimate (49). … In bare forms of trisyllabic verbs, stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (50a-b), but there is a small number of verbs with word-initial stress (50c-d). [p. 40] … Initial stress is lexical; penultimate stress is supplied by the language's phonology in the absence of lexical stress. [p. 41] … Penultimate stress is the language's default assigned to verbs without lexical stress. [p. 42] … Monophthongal nuclei make for monomoraic syllables; diphthongal nuclei make for bimoraic syllables. The glottal stop does not contribute to weight at the foot level, but attracts stress to the syllable which contains the second mora to its left. [p. 10]
sources.locator: §4.2 'verbal classes', printed pp. 40-42 (PDF pp. 45-47); weight statement §2.4 p. 10 (PDF p. 15); glottal-stress statement §1.1 p. 2 (PDF p. 7); review of Borman/F&H/Repetti-Ludlow §2.2.2 pp. 6-7 (PDF pp. 11-12)
sources.note: First-hand fieldwork description of VERBAL stress. Default primary stress is penultimate for lexically stressless verbs (di- and trisyllabic alike; monosyllables pattern with these); a lexical class of verbs has fixed word-initial stress (ááfa 'speak', páña 'hear', ááfase 'insult', kúndase 'tell'). Stress is almost never word-final (p. 15). Syllable weight is moraic (diphthong = 2 moras); a glottal stop attracts stress to the syllable containing the second mora to its left ('glottal stress', pp. 2, 10, §4.5), so a stem-final heavy syllable can bear stress before a glottalised suffix. sources.quote: By default, A'ingae primary stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable of the word. Nevertheless, it is often the case that the position of stress cannot be computed based on surface properties alone, and instead requires reference to the morphological composition of the word. … There are two classes of verbal roots in A'ingae: underlyingly stressless and with underlying word-initial stress. (Underlying stress is always word-initial.) The membership of a verb in either class is unpredictable. Underlyingly stressless verbs are assigned the default penultimate stress (3a-b). Underlying word-initial stress is preserved in the surface forms (3c-d).
sources.note: Same generalisation as the 2019 thesis in peer-reviewed form: default penultimate primary stress (head trochaic foot), unpredictable lexical class with word-initial stress, and four suffix classes (±prestressing, ±dominance) that determine surface stress in morphologically complex verbs.
